attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: A firm present-tense description of the trend. Read in context, this is about GenAI polluting science. The normalisation keeps both the speed and the direction.

contract.note: The plain reading (defective AI material rising fast in early 2024, as opposed to legitimate AI use or faster discovery) is ordinary and fair. Fixing the period to early 2024 is the evaluator's interpretation, but a reasonable one.

evidence.note: Measures LLM-modified text through Feb 2024, not defective or careless content, so it cannot settle the contract's metric.

reviews.rationale: The only item shows LLM use rising, not defective AI content rising. The packet has no comparable audit of validated defective publications in early 2024 against a baseline, so the claim is neither supported nor contradicted.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The scoreable part is the unhedged 'about to destroy' embedded in a policy remark, and the tax proposal is rightly left out. The wording is close to hyperbole, but it is firm language predicting imminence with no date.

contract.note: Reading 'destroy' as functional collapse of peer review is the ordinary sense of the word. With no calendar deadline, continued operation cannot conclusively falsify the forecast. That is a fair treatment of an undated 'about to'.

evidence.note: A 2026 Springer Nature statement about itself describing peer review still operating. It weighs against collapse but cannot conclusively resolve an undated forecast.
Documents GPT-fabricated papers circulating and warns of risks. It does not show journal review being destroyed.

reviews.rationale: No dated evidence shows peer review collapsing or ceasing because of LLM material. Peer review continuing to operate counts against the forecast, but the claim has no deadline and the early-resolution rule has not been met, so it stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Is going to' is firm, even though the sentences around it are hedged. Saying 'bad LLM-generated papers' for 'bad stuff' is a slight narrowing, and the contract handles it by counting defective material.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair and ordinary: many distinct published papers whose LLM-linked defects (such as fabricated references) got past review. Counting peer-reviewed CS conference proceedings is reasonable.

evidence.note: Human-verified hallucinated citations in more than 51 accepted NeurIPS 2025 papers, published Jan 2026. These are distinct post-forecast publications that passed peer review. GPTZero sells detection tools, and LLM origin is inferred from the error patterns.
Finds 85.3% of hallucinated references in preprints persist into journal versions. This corroborates the failure mode, but the sample spans several years and is not a clean post-forecast count.

reviews.rationale: A dated audit (e4, Jan 2026) documents dozens of distinct post-forecast peer-reviewed papers with verified fabricated citations that got past reviewers. That meets the early-resolution rule. e5 points the same way for journals, and the packet contains no counterevidence.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'No way ... going to be able to' is a firm forecast. In context, the flood refers to GenAI-driven submissions. The tripling example is only an illustration.

contract.note: Reading 'keep up' as broad, sustained loss of review capacity or effective screening is an ordinary reading. Treating isolated errors as insufficient is fair to the speaker's broad claim.

evidence.note: A May 2024 interview describing difficulty recruiting reviewers at AI conferences. It does not show journals failing system-wide or isolate the LLM effect.
Springer Nature's own unaudited annual report claims review is operating at scale. It weighs against incapacity but is not an independent finding.

reviews.rationale: The claim has no deadline, and no dated evidence shows sustained breakdown across publishers attributable to LLM submissions. The publisher's own reports of continued operation do not resolve it either, so it stays open.
